item.title: Interactive network graphs in JavaScript with CanvasXpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
A network graph shows relationships: nodes connected by edges, laid out so connected things sit near each other. In the browser the common answer is to hand-roll a force simulation in D3 — a few hundred lines. CanvasXpress is a JavaScript library at heart, so the whole thing is a data object of nodes and edges plus a config.

Load the library

<link href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@73.3.0/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.css" rel="stylesheet">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@73.3.0/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.min.js"></script>

The markup and the spec

Nodes carry id, name, group; edges carry id1, id2, value. colorNodeBy colours by community and networkLayoutType: "forceDirected" runs the physics.

<canvas id="network" width="650" height="500"></canvas>
<script>
  var groups = ["Alpha", "Beta", "Gamma"], nodes = [], byGroup = {}, k = 0;
  groups.forEach(function (g) {
    byGroup[g] = [];
    for (var i = 0; i < 7; i++) {
      var nid = "n" + k; nodes.push({ id: nid, name: g + (i + 1), group: g });
      byGroup[g].push(nid); k++;
    }
  });

  var edges = [];
  groups.forEach(function (g) {                         // dense within a community
    var m = byGroup[g];
    for (var i = 0; i < m.length; i++)
      for (var j = i + 1; j < m.length; j++)
        if (Math.random() < 0.5)
          edges.push({ id1: m[i], id2: m[j], value: 1 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 5) });
  });
  for (var e = 0; e < 6; e++) {                         // a few cross-community links
    var pair = groups.slice().sort(function () { return Math.random() - 0.5; }).slice(0, 2);
    var a = byGroup[pair[0]], b = byGroup[pair[1]];
    edges.push({ id1: a[Math.floor(Math.random() * a.length)],
                 id2: b[Math.floor(Math.random() * b.length)], value: 1 });
  }

  var config = {
    graphType: "Network",
    networkLayoutType: "forceDirected",
    colorNodeBy: "group",
    nodeSize: 25,
    showAnimation: true,
    title: "A small community network"
  };

  new CanvasXpress("network", { nodes: nodes, edges: edges }, config);
</script>

Live result

Drag any node and the layout settles around it; hover to read the label. The three communities separate on their own because within-group edges outnumber the cross-group ones.

Why “reproducible”

The nodes, edges and config are the figure — one portable JSON spec that renders the same from R, Python, or a web page.

item.title: Genome browser tracks in JavaScript with CanvasXpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
A genome browser view stacks tracks that share one coordinate axis: coverage, gene models, variants. Building one in the browser by hand is a lot of SVG and coordinate math. CanvasXpress is a JavaScript library at heart, so the whole view is a data object of tracks plus a config.

Load the library

<link href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@73.3.0/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.css" rel="stylesheet">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@73.3.0/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.min.js"></script>

The markup and the spec

Four tracks that share one coordinate axis: gene models (box, multi-exon, connected), coverage across three tissues (bar), an expression heatmap (heatmap), and variant markers (triangle).

<canvas id="genome" width="760" height="520"></canvas>
<script>
  // Gene models: each gene is a set of exon [start, end] intervals, drawn connected.
  var genes = [];
  for (var j = 0; j < 4; j++) {
    var start = 40 + j * 120, nex = 2 + Math.floor(Math.random() * 3), exons = [];
    for (var k = 0; k < nex; k++) exons.push([start + k * 30, start + k * 30 + 18]);
    genes.push({ id: "GENE" + (j + 1), dir: j % 2 === 0 ? "right" : "left",
                 fill: "rgb(70,130,220)", outline: "rgb(0,0,0)", data: exons });
  }

  // Coverage and expression: one entry per binned position, three tissues each.
  var coverage = [], express = [], rnd = function (a, b) { return a + Math.floor(Math.random() * (b - a + 1)); };
  for (var i = 0; i < 22; i++) {
    var o = 50 + i * 22;
    coverage.push({ id: "p" + i, offset: o, data: [rnd(8, 45), rnd(8, 45), rnd(8, 45)] });
    express.push({ id: "p" + i, offset: o,
                   data: [Math.round(Math.random() * 4 - 2), Math.round(Math.random() * 4 - 2),
                          Math.round(Math.random() * 4 - 2)] });
  }

  // Variants: point markers at genomic positions.
  var snps = [];
  for (var s = 0; s < 9; s++)
    snps.push({ id: "rs" + (1000 + s), offset: rnd(45, 520), fill: "rgb(200,40,40)", outline: "rgb(0,0,0)" });

  var data = { tracks: [
    { name: "Genes (exon models)", type: "box", connect: true, data: genes },
    { name: "Coverage — Heart / Liver / Kidney", type: "bar", height: 120,
      fill: "rgb(80,80,200)", outline: "rgb(60,60,60)", data: coverage },
    { name: "Expression (z-score)", type: "heatmap", height: 90, data: express },
    { name: "SNPs", type: "triangle", data: snps }
  ]};

  var config = { graphType: "Genome", background: "rgb(245,245,245)", featureStaggered: true,
                 title: "Multi-track genome browser: genes, coverage, expression and variants" };

  new CanvasXpress("genome", data, config);
</script>

Live result

Scroll/drag to pan and zoom into a region; every track stays locked to the shared coordinate axis, so the gene models, coverage, expression and variants line up position-for-position. Swap each track for your own pileup, annotation and VCF-derived data.

Why “reproducible”

The tracks and config are the figure — one portable JSON spec that renders the same from R, Python, or a web page.

item.title: An interactive NGS sequencing-QC dashboard in JavaScript with CanvasXpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
After a sequencing run you get a QC table — one row per sample, a dozen metrics — and you need to answer three questions fast: which samples fail, is a whole batch off, and are the failures correlated? A single scatter can’t do it; you want several views that talk to each other — select a suspicious sample in one and see it light up in the rest. In the browser that usually means wiring event handlers between chart libraries by hand. CanvasXpress does it for you: give every panel the same broadcast group and a selection broadcasts to all of them. Here we build a real QC dashboard for 96 RNA/exome samples.

Load the library and the data

The 96-sample QC table is published next to this post as a small JS object, qc-data.js — QC_DATA is a sample-centric CanvasXpress data object (each sample is a point; z holds its lane/batch/library).

<link href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@73.3.0/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.css" rel="stylesheet">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@73.3.0/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.min.js"></script>
<script src="qc-data.js"></script>

The panels

The overview heatmap transposes the data to metrics × samples and z-scores each metric. The four triage panels read QC_DATA directly and all share broadcastGroup: "qc" — select points in one and the same samples re-mark in the rest.

<canvas id="qcHeat" width="820" height="420"></canvas>
<canvas id="qcMap" width="640" height="360"></canvas>
<canvas id="qcContam" width="640" height="360"></canvas>
<canvas id="qcQ30" width="640" height="360"></canvas>
<canvas id="qcReads" width="820" height="300"></canvas>
<script>
  var metrics = QC_DATA.y.smps, samples = QC_DATA.y.vars, rows = QC_DATA.y.data;

  // Overview: transpose to metrics x samples and z-score each metric.
  var hmData = metrics.map(function (_, c) {
    var col = rows.map(function (r) { return r[c]; });
    var mean = col.reduce(function (a, b) { return a + b; }, 0) / col.length;
    var sd = Math.sqrt(col.reduce(function (a, b) { return a + (b - mean) * (b - mean); }, 0) / col.length) || 1;
    return col.map(function (v) { return Math.round((v - mean) / sd * 100) / 100; });
  });
  new CanvasXpress("qcHeat",
    { y: { vars: metrics, smps: samples, data: hmData },
      x: { Batch: QC_DATA.z.Batch, Library: QC_DATA.z.Library } },
    { graphType: "Heatmap", samplesClustered: true, variablesClustered: true,
      colorSpectrum: ["navy", "white", "firebrick3"],
      title: "QC metrics (z-scored) — 96 samples clustered" });

  // Linked triage panels (same QC_DATA, shared broadcast group).
  function panel(id, cfg) {
    new CanvasXpress(id, QC_DATA, Object.assign({ broadcast: true, broadcastGroup: "qc" }, cfg));
  }
  panel("qcMap", { graphType: "Scatter2D", xAxis: ["pct_duplication"], yAxis: ["pct_mapped"],
    colorBy: "Batch", sizeBy: "total_reads", title: "Mapping rate vs duplication — select bottom-right" });
  panel("qcContam", { graphType: "Scatter2D", xAxis: ["pct_mapped"], yAxis: ["contamination_freemix"],
    colorBy: "Batch", title: "Contamination (freemix) vs mapping rate" });
  panel("qcQ30", { graphType: "Scatter2D", xAxis: ["gc_content"], yAxis: ["pct_q30"],
    colorBy: "Library", title: "Q30 vs GC content, coloured by library" });
  panel("qcReads", { graphType: "Bar", graphOrientation: "vertical", xAxis: ["total_reads"],
    colorBy: "Batch", title: "Total reads per sample (flag the short ones)" });
</script>

Live result

Drag a selection box across the bad cluster in the mapping-vs-duplication panel — the other panels restrict to the same samples so you can read their contamination, library and depth.

The cross-filter is one shared broadcastGroup — no framework, no event wiring. Each panel stays a portable data + config spec.

Why “reproducible”

The same specs reproduce the dashboard from R, Python, or a web page, against the same QC table.

item.title: Interactive network graphs in Python with canvasxpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
A network graph shows relationships: nodes connected by edges, laid out so connected things sit near each other. The usual Python reach is networkx + matplotlib (static) or pyvis. Here we build one with canvasxpress — draggable, hover-labelled, force-directed, and reproducible from a single portable spec.

Install

pip install canvasxpress

The data shape

canvasXpress builds a network from two lists: nodes (id, name, group) and edges (id1, id2, value). Swap this simulated three-community graph for your own.

import random
random.seed(1)

groups = ["Alpha", "Beta", "Gamma"]
nodes, by_group = [], {g: [] for g in groups}
k = 0
for g in groups:
    for i in range(7):
        nid = f"n{k}"; nodes.append({"id": nid, "name": f"{g}{i+1}", "group": g})
        by_group[g].append(nid); k += 1

edges = []
for g in groups:                                   # dense within a community
    m = by_group[g]
    for i in range(len(m)):
        for j in range(i + 1, len(m)):
            if random.random() < 0.5:
                edges.append({"id1": m[i], "id2": m[j], "value": random.randint(1, 5)})
for _ in range(6):                                 # a few cross-community links
    g1, g2 = random.sample(groups, 2)
    edges.append({"id1": random.choice(by_group[g1]), "id2": random.choice(by_group[g2]), "value": 1})

The plot

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {"nodes": nodes, "edges": edges}
config = {
    "graphType": "Network",
    "networkLayoutType": "forceDirected",
    "colorNodeBy": "group",
    "nodeSize": 25,
    "showAnimation": True,
    "title": "A small community network",
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="network", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=500)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)

Drag any node and the layout settles around it; hover to read the label. The three communities separate on their own because within-group edges outnumber the cross-group ones.

Why “reproducible”

The nodes, edges and config are the figure — one portable JSON spec that renders the identical network from R or JavaScript, and can be validated and re-rendered later.

item.title: An interactive NGS sequencing-QC dashboard in Python with canvasxpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
After a sequencing run you get a QC table — one row per sample, a dozen metrics — and you need to answer three questions fast: which samples fail, is a whole batch off, and are the failures correlated? A single scatter can’t do it; you want several views that talk to each other — select a suspicious sample in one and see it light up in the rest. In Python that usually means Dash or Streamlit (a server, callbacks). canvasXpress does it client-side: give every panel the same broadcast group and a selection broadcasts to all of them. Here we build a real QC dashboard for 96 RNA/exome samples.

Install

pip install canvasxpress

The QC table

96 samples with mapping rate, duplication, Q30, GC, insert size and contamination (VerifyBamID freemix), plus lane / batch / library annotations. (Download: ngs-qc.csv.)

import csv, statistics as st

rows = list(csv.DictReader(open("ngs-qc.csv")))
metrics = ["total_reads", "pct_mapped", "pct_duplication", "pct_q30",
           "gc_content", "insert_size", "contamination_freemix"]

samples = [r["sample"] for r in rows]
annot   = {"Lane": [r["lane"] for r in rows], "Batch": [r["batch"] for r in rows],
           "Library": [r["library"] for r in rows]}
raw = {m: [float(r[m]) for r in rows] for m in metrics}
print(len(samples), "samples,", len(metrics), "metrics")
96 samples, 7 metrics

Overview — a clustered QC heatmap

Z-score each metric and cluster: outlier samples and any batch/library structure jump out at a glance. This is the “is anything wrong, and where” view. Here the matrix is metrics × samples.

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

z = {m: [(v - st.mean(raw[m])) / (st.pstdev(raw[m]) or 1) for v in raw[m]] for m in metrics}
hm = {"y": {"vars": metrics, "smps": samples, "data": [[round(x, 2) for x in z[m]] for m in metrics]},
      "x": {"Batch": annot["Batch"], "Library": annot["Library"]}}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="qcHeat", data=hm, width=820, height=420, config={
    "graphType": "Heatmap", "samplesClustered": True, "variablesClustered": True,
    "colorSpectrum": ["navy", "white", "firebrick3"],
    "title": "QC metrics (z-scored) — 96 samples clustered"})
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)

The linked triage dashboard

Four panels over the same samples, all sharing broadcastGroup: "qc". The sample is the unit, so each sample is a point and its lane/batch/library live in the per-sample annotation z. Select points in any panel and the same samples re-mark everywhere.

# Sample-centric: vars = samples (points), smps = metrics (axes), z = per-sample annotations.
data = {"y": {"vars": samples, "smps": metrics, "data": [[raw[m][i] for m in metrics] for i in range(len(samples))]},
        "z": annot}

def panel(cfg, cid, w=640, h=360):
    cfg = {**cfg, "broadcast": True, "broadcastGroup": "qc"}
    cx = CanvasXpress(render_to=cid, data=data, config=cfg, width=w, height=h)
    for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
        display(part)

1 — Mapping rate vs duplication (the triage plot)

Bubble size is depth; failing libraries fall to the bottom-right. Lasso them here.

panel({"graphType": "Scatter2D", "xAxis": ["pct_duplication"], "yAxis": ["pct_mapped"],
       "colorBy": "Batch", "sizeBy": "total_reads",
       "title": "Mapping rate vs duplication — select the bottom-right"}, "qcMap")

2 — Contamination vs mapping

panel({"graphType": "Scatter2D", "xAxis": ["pct_mapped"], "yAxis": ["contamination_freemix"],
       "colorBy": "Batch", "title": "Contamination (freemix) vs mapping rate"}, "qcContam")

3 — Q30 vs GC, by library prep

panel({"graphType": "Scatter2D", "xAxis": ["gc_content"], "yAxis": ["pct_q30"],
       "colorBy": "Library", "title": "Q30 vs GC content, coloured by library"}, "qcQ30")

4 — Sequencing depth per sample

panel({"graphType": "Bar", "graphOrientation": "vertical", "xAxis": ["total_reads"],
       "colorBy": "Batch", "title": "Total reads per sample (flag the short ones)"}, "qcReads", w=820, h=300)

Lasso the bad cluster in panel 1 and panels 2–4 immediately restrict to those samples — you can read their contamination, library and depth without a single callback. The “wiring” is one shared group id.

Why “reproducible”

Each panel is a portable data + config spec; the cross-filter is just a shared broadcastGroup. The same specs reproduce the dashboard from R or JavaScript, against the same ngs-qc.csv.

item.title: Genome browser tracks in Python with canvasxpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
A genome browser view stacks tracks that share one coordinate axis: coverage, gene models, variants. In Python this usually means pyGenomeTracks or a static matplotlib figure. Here we build an interactive, zoomable view with canvasxpress — from one portable spec.

Install

pip install canvasxpress

The data shape

A Genome figure is a list of tracks that share one coordinate axis — each with a type. Real browser views stack several: here we build four — gene models (box, multi-exon, connected), coverage across three tissues (bar), an expression heatmap (heatmap), and variant markers (triangle).

import random
random.seed(3)

# Gene models: each gene is a set of exon [start, end] intervals, drawn connected.
genes = []
for j in range(4):
    start = 40 + j * 120
    exons = [[start + k * 30, start + k * 30 + 18] for k in range(random.randint(2, 4))]
    genes.append({"id": f"GENE{j+1}", "dir": "right" if j % 2 == 0 else "left",
                  "fill": "rgb(70,130,220)", "outline": "rgb(0,0,0)", "data": exons})

# Coverage and expression: one entry per binned position, three tissues each.
offsets  = [50 + i * 22 for i in range(22)]
coverage = [{"id": f"p{i}", "offset": o,
             "data": [random.randint(8, 45), random.randint(8, 45), random.randint(8, 45)]}
            for i, o in enumerate(offsets)]
express  = [{"id": f"p{i}", "offset": o,
             "data": [round(random.gauss(0, 1), 2) for _ in range(3)]}
            for i, o in enumerate(offsets)]

# Variants: point markers at genomic positions.
snps = [{"id": f"rs{1000+k}", "offset": random.randint(45, 520),
         "fill": "rgb(200,40,40)", "outline": "rgb(0,0,0)"} for k in range(9)]

data = {"tracks": [
    {"name": "Genes (exon models)", "type": "box", "connect": True, "data": genes},
    {"name": "Coverage — Heart / Liver / Kidney", "type": "bar", "height": 120,
     "fill": "rgb(80,80,200)", "outline": "rgb(60,60,60)", "data": coverage},
    {"name": "Expression (z-score)", "type": "heatmap", "height": 90, "data": express},
    {"name": "SNPs", "type": "triangle", "data": snps},
]}

The plot

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

config = {
    "graphType": "Genome",
    "background": "rgb(245,245,245)",
    "featureStaggered": True,
    "title": "Multi-track genome browser: genes, coverage, expression and variants",
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="genome", data=data, config=config, width=760, height=520)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)

Scroll/drag to pan and zoom into a region; every track stays locked to the shared coordinate axis, so the gene models, coverage, expression and variants line up position-for-position. Swap each track for your own pileup, annotation and VCF-derived data.

Why “reproducible”

The tracks and config are the figure — one portable JSON spec that renders the identical browser view from R or JavaScript, and can be validated and re-rendered later.

item.title: Interactive network graphs in R with canvasXpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
A network graph shows relationships: nodes connected by edges, laid out so that connected things sit near each other. The usual R reach is igraph or networkD3, but here we build one with canvasXpress — draggable, hover-labelled, force-directed, and reproducible, because the whole figure is one portable data + config spec.

The data shape

canvasXpress builds a network from two tables: nodes (id, name, group) and edges (id1, id2, value). Swap this simulated three-community graph for your own.

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(1)
grp   <- rep(c("Alpha", "Beta", "Gamma"), each = 7)
ids   <- paste0("n", seq_along(grp))
nodes <- data.frame(id = ids, name = paste0(grp, ave(grp, grp, FUN = seq_along)),
                    group = grp, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

# Dense within a community, sparse between communities — the structure a layout reveals.
e1 <- c(); e2 <- c(); ev <- c()
for (g in unique(grp)) {
  m <- ids[grp == g]
  for (i in seq_along(m)) for (j in seq_along(m))
    if (i < j && runif(1) < 0.5) { e1 <- c(e1, m[i]); e2 <- c(e2, m[j]); ev <- c(ev, sample(1:5, 1)) }
}
for (k in 1:6) {                                     # a few cross-community links
  pair <- sample(unique(grp), 2)
  e1 <- c(e1, sample(ids[grp == pair[1]], 1)); e2 <- c(e2, sample(ids[grp == pair[2]], 1)); ev <- c(ev, 1)
}
edges <- data.frame(id1 = e1, id2 = e2, value = ev, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)

The plot

Pass the two tables as nodeData and edgeData; colorNodeBy colours by the community, and networkLayoutType = "forceDirected" runs the physics simulation.

canvasXpress(
  nodeData          = nodes,
  edgeData          = edges,
  graphType         = "Network",
  networkLayoutType = "forceDirected",
  colorNodeBy       = "group",
  nodeSize          = 25,
  showAnimation     = TRUE,
  title             = "A small community network",
  width             = 650,
  height            = 500
)

Drag any node and the layout settles around it; hover to read the label. The three communities separate on their own because within-group edges outnumber the cross-group ones.

Why “reproducible”

The nodes, edges and config are the figure — one portable specification. The same spec renders the identical network from Python or JavaScript, and can be validated and re-rendered later.

After a sequencing run you get a QC table — one row per sample, a dozen metrics — and you need to answer three questions fast: which samples fail, is a whole batch off, and are the failures correlated? library(canvasXpress)

qc <- read.csv("ngs-qc.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
metrics <- c("total_reads", "pct_mapped", "pct_duplication", "pct_q30",
             "gc_content", "insert_size", "contamination_freemix")

m        <- as.matrix(qc[, metrics]); rownames(m) <- qc$sample
annot    <- data.frame(Lane = qc$lane, Batch = qc$batch, Library = qc$library,
                      row.names = qc$sample)
head(qc[, c("sample", "batch", "library", "pct_mapped", "pct_duplication",
            "contamination_freemix")], 4)
  sample batch  library pct_mapped pct_duplication contamination_freemix
1   S001  RunA    PolyA      93.85           11.90                0.0165
2   S002  RunC RiboZero      86.82           13.41                0.0015
3   S003  RunA RiboZero      99.47            7.88                0.0205

Overview — a clustered QC heatmap

Z-score each metric and cluster: outlier samples and any batch/library structure jump out at a glance. This is the “is anything wrong, and where” view.

canvasXpress(

item.title: Genome browser tracks in R with canvasXpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
A genome browser view stacks tracks that share one coordinate axis: coverage, gene models, variants. In R this usually means Gviz or ggbio. Here we build an interactive, zoomable view with canvasXpress — and the whole thing is one portable spec.

The data shape

A Genome figure is a list of tracks that share one coordinate axis — each with a type. Real browser views stack several: here we build four — gene models (box, multi-exon, connected), coverage across three tissues (bar), an expression heatmap (heatmap), and variant markers (triangle).

library(canvasXpress)

set.seed(3)

# Gene models: each gene is a set of exon [start, end] intervals, drawn connected.
genes <- lapply(0:3, function(j) {
  start <- 40 + j * 120
  exons <- lapply(0:(sample(2:4, 1) - 1), function(k) list(start + k * 30, start + k * 30 + 18))
  list(id = paste0("GENE", j + 1), dir = if (j %% 2 == 0) "right" else "left",
       fill = "rgb(70,130,220)", outline = "rgb(0,0,0)", data = exons)
})

# Coverage and expression: one entry per binned position, three tissues each.
offsets  <- 50 + (0:21) * 22
coverage <- lapply(seq_along(offsets), function(i)
  list(id = paste0("p", i), offset = offsets[i],
       data = list(sample(8:45, 1), sample(8:45, 1), sample(8:45, 1))))
express  <- lapply(seq_along(offsets), function(i)
  list(id = paste0("p", i), offset = offsets[i],
       data = list(round(rnorm(1), 2), round(rnorm(1), 2), round(rnorm(1), 2))))

# Variants: point markers at genomic positions.
snps <- lapply(0:8, function(k)
  list(id = paste0("rs", 1000 + k), offset = sample(45:520, 1),
       fill = "rgb(200,40,40)", outline = "rgb(0,0,0)"))

genome <- list(tracks = list(
  list(name = "Genes (exon models)", type = "box", connect = TRUE, data = genes),
  list(name = "Coverage — Heart / Liver / Kidney", type = "bar", height = 120,
       fill = "rgb(80,80,200)", outline = "rgb(60,60,60)", data = coverage),
  list(name = "Expression (z-score)", type = "heatmap", height = 90, data = express),
  list(name = "SNPs", type = "triangle", data = snps)
))

The plot

The Genome graph type is passed through to the engine as-is; featureStaggered spreads crowded features so labels stay legible.

canvasXpress(
  data            = genome,
  graphType       = "Genome",
  background       = "rgb(245,245,245)",
  featureStaggered = TRUE,
  title            = "Multi-track genome browser: genes, coverage, expression and variants",
  width            = 760,
  height           = 520
)
The Genome graphType is an advanced chart, data is passed as-is to the JS library

Scroll/drag to pan and zoom into a region; every track stays locked to the shared coordinate axis, so the gene models, coverage, expression and variants line up position-for-position. Swap each track for your own pileup, annotation and VCF-derived data.

item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
A choropleth shades each region by a value — emissions, incidence, turnout, income. It is the most common map in data analysis and the easiest to get subtly wrong: most “my map is all one colour” complaints are not rendering bugs but scale bugs. CanvasXpress does the join and the colouring inside the render, so in the browser you pass one value per region and a topoJSON of boundaries and get an interactive, reproducible figure — and with the right colour scale it stays vivid on exactly the kind of heavy-tailed data that flattens naive maps.

First, the trap: colour encodes a rate, not a count

A choropleth fills an area, and area is a size channel your eye cannot help reading. Shade regions by a raw count — total cases, total emissions, total sales — and big, populous regions light up simply because they are big and populous. You have drawn a population map with extra steps. The fix is almost always to map a rate or density (per capita, per 100k); reserve raw counts for a proportional-symbol map, where a sized bubble carries the count honestly.

Load the library

<link href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@71.3.0/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.css" rel="stylesheet">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@71.3.0/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.min.js"></script>

The markup and the spec

The columns (smps) are the regions — they match the map by name — and the single row (vars) is the variable you colour by: CO₂ emissions per country for 2018. We fetch a prepared table and a small annotation table (continent, ISO code), parse the tab-separated text, and hand the matrix to CanvasXpress. The two choices that make this map work are in the colour scale: a seven-stop viridis colorSpectrum, and colorSpectrumBreaksMethod: "quantile", which puts an equal number of countries in every colour class — on skewed data that guarantee is what keeps all seven colours on the map.

<canvas id="co2quant" width="760" height="520"></canvas>
<script>
  var DATA = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-dat.txt";
  var SMP  = "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/r/cX-CO2-smp.txt";

  // split a tab-separated file into a list of cell-arrays (one per row)
  function rows(text) {
    return text.trim().split("\n").map(function (line) { return line.split("\t"); });
  }

  Promise.all([fetch(DATA).then(function (r) { return r.text(); }),
               fetch(SMP ).then(function (r) { return r.text(); })])
    .then(function (texts) {
      var d = rows(texts[0]);                      // [header, ["CO2", v1, v2, ...]]
      var countries = d[0].slice(1);               // header, minus the empty corner cell
      var values    = d[1].slice(1).map(Number);   // the CO2 values

      var s = rows(texts[1]);                       // header + one row per country
      var col = {};                                 // header name -> column index
      s[0].forEach(function (name, i) { col[name] = i; });
      var byCountry = {};
      s.slice(1).forEach(function (r) { byCountry[r[0]] = r; });
      var continent = countries.map(function (c) { return byCountry[c][col["Continent"] + 1]; });

      var data = {
        y: { vars: ["CO2"], smps: countries, data: [values] },
        x: { Continent: continent }
      };
      var config = {
        graphType: "Map",
        colorBy: "CO2",
        topoJSON: "https://www.canvasxpress.org/data/maps/WORLD.json",
        mapId: "co2Quantile",
        colorSpectrum: ["#440154", "#443983", "#31688e", "#21918c",
                        "#35b779", "#90d743", "#fde725"],
        colorSpectrumBreaksMethod: "quantile",
        mapColor: "#d9dde3",
        mapOutlineColor: "#ffffff",
        legendPosition: "bottom",
        title: "CO2 emissions per country (2018)",
        subtitle: "Seven quantile classes: each colour holds about 28 of 198 countries"
      };
      new CanvasXpress("co2quant", data, config);
    });
</script>

Live result

Every band of the ramp is doing work: the darkest purples are the smallest emitters, the yellows the largest, and the legend’s break values tell you the class edges are data-driven, not evenly spaced. Hover any country for its name, continent and value.

Why not just a plain linear ramp?

Because the data is heavy-tailed — a few countries emit thousands of megatonnes while most emit almost nothing. On a linear scale, 195 of these 198 countries fall into the bottom fifth of the range, so a continuous ramp paints nearly the whole world one pale tone and spends its colour on two or three outliers. See for yourself — same data, default scale:

This is the single most common choropleth failure. The cure is classing:

  • colorSpectrumBreaksMethod: "quantile" — equal counts per class. Every colour is used, by construction. The right default for skewed data and for “which regions rank high/low” questions.
  • colorSpectrumBreaksMethod: "jenks" — natural breaks that minimise within-class variance. Best when the data has genuine clusters with gaps between them; on smoothly heavy-tailed data like this it piles almost everything into the bottom class, so check the legend before you trust it.
  • Three to seven classes is the usable range — beyond that, readers cannot match colours to the legend.

Choose the palette on purpose

The palette is the scale’s grammar, not decoration:

  • Sequential (dark → light of ordered hues, like viridis above) for a quantity that only goes up: counts, rates, concentrations.

  • Diverging (two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint) when values are meaningful above and below a reference: change vs. last year, difference from a target, a signed index. Use a three-colour colorSpectrum and pin the midpoint:

    colorBy: "Change",
colorSpectrum: ["#2166ac", "#f7f7f7", "#b2182b"],  // blue - neutral - red
colorSpectrumZeroValue: 0                           // value mapped to the middle colour

    Never use a diverging palette for a purely positive quantity — the neutral midpoint invents a “normal” the data does not have. Viridis and the ColorBrewer ramps are colour-blind-safe and perceptually ordered; a rainbow ramp is neither. Keep the same scale across small multiples so maps stay comparable.

Beyond the world map

  • Other boundaries. Point topoJSON at any shape file — US states, a country’s provinces, counties, custom districts. The join key is just the shape name.
  • Projection. mapProjection: "albers" (equal-area) or "mercator". Equal-area projections matter for choropleths: Mercator inflates high latitudes and exaggerates their visual weight.
  • Categorical maps. Point colorBy at a categorical field for a qualitative choropleth with a discrete legend.
  • Polish. legendNumberFormat formats the ticks, legendInside floats the legend over ocean, showMapLabels draws region names (best on few-region maps), mapColor sets the no-data fill so missing reads as missing, and decorations drops labelled markers on cities.

The whole figure — data, boundaries, classing rule and palette — is one portable spec you can re-render from R or Python.

The palette is not decoration — it is the scale’s grammar:

  • Sequential (dark → light of ordered hues, like viridis above) for a quantity that only goes up: counts, rates, concentrations.

  • Diverging (two hues meeting at a neutral midpoint) when values are meaningful above and below a reference: change vs. last year, difference from a target, a signed index. Give canvasXpress a three-colour colorSpectrum and pin the midpoint with colorSpectrumZeroValue:

    colorBy = "Change",
colorSpectrum = list("#2166ac", "#f7f7f7", "#b2182b"),  # blue - neutral - red
colorSpectrumZeroValue = 0                               # value mapped to the middle colour

    Never use a diverging palette for a purely positive quantity — the neutral midpoint invents a “normal” that the data does not have.

Viridis and the ColorBrewer ramps are colour-blind-safe and perceptually ordered; a rainbow ramp is neither, so readers cannot tell which end means “more”. Keep the same scale across small multiples so maps stay comparable.

Polish: legend, labels and base styling

  • subtitle / source — caption the units and provenance.
  • legendNumberFormat = list(style = "decimal", decimals = 1, suffix = "%") — format the legend ticks as percentages, currency, etc.
  • mapColor / mapOutlineColor — the fill for regions with no data (a neutral grey) and the border between shapes, so missing data reads as missing rather than as a value.
  • showMapLabels = TRUE — draw region names (best on maps with few regions, e.g. a single country’s provinces; it clutters a 190-country world map).
  • legendInside = TRUE — float the legend over empty ocean to reclaim width.

Beyond the world map

  • Other boundaries. Point topoJSON at any shape file — US states, a single country’s regions, counties, custom districts. The join key is just the shape name.
  • Projection. mapProjection = "albers" (equal-area, good for the US) or "mercator". Equal-area projections matter for choropleths: Mercator inflates high latitudes, exaggerating those regions’ visual weight.
  • Categorical maps. Point colorBy at a categorical column (an election winner, a priority tier) for a qualitative choropleth with a discrete legend.
  • Markers. Add decorations to drop labelled points on cities or call out specific regions.

The whole figure — data, boundaries, classing rule and palette — travels together as one spec, so a reviewer can reproduce it exactly and a colleague can re-render it from Python or JavaScript.

item.title: Violin and half (split) violin plots in JavaScript with CanvasXpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
A violin plot shows the full shape of a distribution instead of collapsing it to a box’s quartiles. And a split (half) violin puts one condition on each half so you can compare two groups at the same position. CanvasXpress is a JavaScript library at heart, so in the browser it’s just a data object and a config.

Load the library

<link href="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@69.6.1/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.css" rel="stylesheet">
<script src="https://cdn.jsdelivr.net/gh/neuhausi/canvasXpress@69.6.1/inst/htmlwidgets/lib/canvasXpress/canvasXpress.min.js"></script>

The markup and the spec

A violin is a Boxplot graph with the violin turned on. One measured variable (value) × N observations, with the grouping columns as sample annotations (x). For the split violin, group by both factors, colour by condition, and set violinSide: "split".

<canvas id="violin" width="650" height="500"></canvas>
<canvas id="violinSplit" width="650" height="500"></canvas>
<script>
  // standard normal via Box–Muller
  function gauss() {
    var u = 0, v = 0;
    while (u === 0) u = Math.random();
    while (v === 0) v = Math.random();
    return Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * v);
  }

  var doses = ["Low", "Medium", "High"], conds = ["Control", "Treated"];
  var mus = { Low: 6, Medium: 8, High: 10 };
  var value = [], Dose = [], Condition = [];
  doses.forEach(function (d) {
    conds.forEach(function (co) {
      var mu = mus[d] + (co === "Treated" ? 1.5 : 0);
      for (var i = 0; i < 40; i++) {
        value.push(Math.round((mu + 1.2 * gauss()) * 100) / 100);
        Dose.push(d); Condition.push(co);
      }
    });
  });
  var ids = value.map(function (_, i) { return "o" + (i + 1); });

  var data = { y: { vars: ["value"], smps: ids, data: [value] },
               x: { Dose: Dose, Condition: Condition } };

  // full violin
  new CanvasXpress("violin", data, {
    graphType: "Boxplot", showViolinBoxplot: true, violinScale: "area",
    groupingFactors: ["Dose"], xAxis: ["value"], smpTitle: "Dose",
    title: "Distribution of value by dose"
  });

  // split (half) violin comparing conditions
  new CanvasXpress("violinSplit", data, {
    graphType: "Boxplot", showViolinBoxplot: true, violinScale: "area",
    groupingFactors: ["Dose", "Condition"], colorBy: "Condition",
    violinSide: "split", violinTrim: false, xAxis: ["value"], smpTitle: "Dose",
    title: "Control vs Treated — split violin by dose"
  });
</script>

Live result

Hover to read the density and summary stats. violinSide can also be "lt" or "rb" for a one-sided half violin.

Why “reproducible”

The data+config is the figure — one portable JSON spec that renders the same from R, Python, or a web page.

item.title: Clustered heatmaps in Python with canvasxpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
The clustered heatmap is the default way to look at an expression matrix: rows and columns reordered by similarity, dendrograms on the margins, and sample metadata alongside. Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — clustering happens inside the render, so you pass a plain matrix and get an interactive, reproducible figure.

Install

pip install canvasxpress

An expression matrix with sample metadata

Swap this simulated block for your own matrix (genes in rows, samples in columns) and a table of per-sample annotations.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd

rng   = np.random.default_rng(1)
ng, ns = 40, 30
genes = [f"Gene{i+1}" for i in range(ng)]
samps = [f"S{i+1}"    for i in range(ns)]
cond  = ["Tumor"] * (ns // 2) + ["Normal"] * (ns // 2)

m = rng.normal(0, 1, (ng, ns))
tumor = [i for i, c in enumerate(cond) if c == "Tumor"]
normal = [i for i, c in enumerate(cond) if c == "Normal"]
m[np.ix_(range(0, 20),  tumor)]  += 2      # first block up in Tumor
m[np.ix_(range(20, 40), normal)] += 2      # second block up in Normal

expr = pd.DataFrame(m.round(3), index=genes, columns=samps)

Build the spec

The matrix goes in as data, and the sample annotation becomes an annotation track over the columns. samplesClustered / variablesClustered turn on hierarchical clustering with dendrograms.

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    "y": {"vars": genes, "smps": samps, "data": expr.values.tolist()},
    "x": {"Condition": cond},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "Heatmap",
    "samplesClustered": True, "variablesClustered": True,
    "colorSpectrum": ["navy", "white", "firebrick3"],
    "showSmpDendrogram": True, "showVarDendrogram": True,
    "title": "Clustered expression heatmap",
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="heatmap", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=550)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)

Rows and columns are reordered by similarity, the dendrograms show the clustering, and the samples separate cleanly by condition. Hover a cell for its gene, sample and value; the whole figure is one portable spec you can store, validate and re-render from R or JavaScript.

item.title: Kaplan–Meier survival curves in Python with canvasxpress
item.dc:creator: Isaac Neuhaus
item.description:
Kaplan–Meier curves summarize time-to-event data: the step-down survival probability over time, usually split by a group like treatment arm. Here we build one in Python with canvasxpress — it computes the survival steps for you from a time column and a censoring column — and the result is interactive and reproducible.

Install

pip install canvasxpress

A survival table

Swap this simulated block for your own data: per subject you need a follow-up time, a censoring indicator (1 = censored, 0 = event), and the grouping variable.

import numpy as np

rng  = np.random.default_rng(1)
n    = 200
arm  = rng.choice(["Treatment", "Control"], n)
base = np.where(arm == "Treatment", 60, 40)     # treatment survives longer
time = np.round(rng.exponential(base), 1)
cens = rng.binomial(1, 0.3, n)                  # 1 = censored, 0 = event
subj = [f"Subj{i+1}" for i in range(n)]

Build the spec

The two columns — the time and its matching censor flag — go in as the variable samples, and the arm rides along as a variable annotation. The key is graphType="KaplanMeier" and passing both columns to xAxis.

from canvasxpress.canvas import CanvasXpress
from canvasxpress.render.jupyter import CXNoteBook
from IPython.display import display

data = {
    # Subjects are the variables (rows); each row holds [Time, Time-Censor].
    "y": {"vars": subj, "smps": ["Time", "Time-Censor"],
          "data": [[t, c] for t, c in zip(time.tolist(), cens.tolist())]},
    "z": {"Arm": arm.tolist()},
}

config = {
    "graphType": "KaplanMeier",
    "xAxis": ["Time", "Time-Censor"],
    "colorBy": "Arm",
    "title": "Overall survival by treatment arm",
    "xAxisTitle": "Time (weeks)", "yAxisTitle": "Probability of survival",
    "invertCensored": True,               # draw censoring ticks
    "showKMConfidenceIntervals": False,
}

cx = CanvasXpress(render_to="km", data=data, config=config, width=650, height=500)
for part in CXNoteBook(cx).render():
    display(part)

Hover any step for the time and survival probability; the tick marks are censored subjects. canvasxpress derives the survival curve from the raw table, so you never precompute the steps — and the same spec re-renders the identical curve from R or JavaScript.

A common gotcha

The survival transform only fires with graphType="KaplanMeier". A bare "Scatter2D" gives a raw scatter of the censor values instead — survival probability is computed by the engine, not a column in your data.
